sentences.text:
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), wherein it is alleged that the accused had sold misbranded food in violation of Section
2 (ix)(d) and (e) of PFA Act, as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.

2. As per the complaint, on 31.10.2010, the food officials including Food Inspector (FI) Geet Ram and Field Assistant (FA) Balwant Shah under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Smt. Usha Chaturvedi reached at the premises of M/s. Tiwari Sweets at 27/37, Gali No.9, Vishwas Nagar, Delhi-110032, where the accused in the capacity of vendor-cum-proprietor was found conducting the business of various food articles, including 'Patisa', which was found stored for sale for human consumption, lying in an open tray bearing no label declaration.
The food officials lifted the sample the said food article consisting of 1500 gm of Patisa ready for sale.
It was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed.
Necessary documents were prepared at the spot including the vendor's receipt and panchanama.
Price of the sample was paid to the vendor.
One counterpart of the sample was deposited with the Public Analyst (PA) and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 06.12.2010, the PA reported that the sample was misbranded as it showed presence of synthetic which was not declared as one of the ingredients.

Based on the report In Re vs Sh. Sumit Tiwari on 31 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82354384/
1 of PA, investigation was carried out by the Food Inspector as per the instructions of the SDM/LHA.

After obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA, the present complaint came to be filed against the accused for violation of the section 2(ix)(d) and (e), as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act for selling misbranded food.
3. Since the complaint was filed by a public servant in writing, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 09.05.2011.

Based on the report of PA, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed vide order dated 25.11.2011 against the accused for commission of offence under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act being in violation of Section 2(ix)(e) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
No notice/charge was framed for violation of section 2(ix)(d) of the Act, though the complaint was filed alleging its violation as well.
4. At the trial, the prosecution examined four witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 FI Jeet Ram,
PW-2 Smt. Usha Trivedi, PW-3 FI Balwant Shah were the part of the team that had visited the premises of accused and lifted the sample of Patisa lying in an open tray bearing no label or declaration.

These witnesses deposed about the sample proceedings conducted by them on 31.10.2010 and narrated the steps undertaken by them, including disclosing their identity, lifting 1500 gms of Patisa, breaking it into smallest possible pieces with the help of a clean and dry knife,
mixing them and dividing the same in three counterparts by putting them in three clean and dry sample glass bottles, adding 40 drops of formalin in each bottle, separately packing, fastening,
marking and sealing them.
A sum of Rs. 225/- was paid to the vendor as price of the sample vide vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-1/ A.
Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C were prepared at the spot.
Raid report Ex. PW- 1/D was also prepared by the FI.
One counterpart was deposited with the PA vide receipt Ex.
PW-1 /
E and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA vide receipt Ex. PW-1/F on the next working day.
PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received opining the sample to be misbranded.

Further investigation was carried out during which letter Ex.
PW-1/H was written to vendor accused but it was not replied.
Letter Ex. PW-1/I was written to STO and its reply Ex. PW-1/J was received.
Further investigation was conducted by PW-4 FI M.K.Gupta.

After completion of investigation, consent for prosecution Ex. PW-2/A was taken from the Director,
PFA, after which the complaint Ex. PW-2/B was filed and intimation letter Ex. PW-4/A was served upon the accused personally against acknowledgement.
These witnesses were duly cross examined by the Ld. Defence Counsel, wherein they denied that the accused was falsely implicated.
5. Statement of the accused was recorded under section 313 CrPC on 10.08.2015 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Accused accepted the proceedings dated 31.10.2010 but claimed that no effort was made to join public witnesses.
He questioned the PA report and claimed that he did not put any colour in the patisa and had used haldi powder.
He did not lead any evidence in defence despite opportunity.

6. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as all the witnesses have supported its case and there is no contradiction in their testimony.
It is submitted that the accused has failed to rebut the findings as given by the PA.

In Re vs Sh. Sumit Tiwari on 31 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82354384/
2 7.
On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused has submitted that the prosecution case fails on technical grounds.
Ld. Counsel for accused has submitted that there is no violation of section 2(ix)(e) of PFA Act as there was no false claim made anywhere by the accused.
It is submitted that no charge has been framed against the accused for violation of section 2(ix)(d) which pertains to colouring, flavouring, coating or polishing the food article.
It is also pointed out that the quantity of the food colour tartrazine has been found to be only 15.22 ppm which is well within permissible limits of 100 ppm.
8. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
9. In a criminal trial, the burden is on the complainant / prosecution to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and has to be necessarily discharged by the prosecution itself by leading cogent and trustworthy evidence.
10. In the present case, there is no serious dispute as to the steps undertaken by PWs in lifting the sample.
All the PWs, who were a part of the team that had lifted the sample, have deposed in corroboration of each other.
No material contradiction can be seen in their testimony that would go to the root of the matter so as to disbelieve them.
All deposed about steps undertaken by them during sample proceedings.
All deposed about compliance of rules while lifting the sample.
No question was put to them regarding non-compliance of any mandatory rule, except putting some general bald suggestions.
All the witnesses deposed that attempt was made to join public persons as witnesses but none had joined.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
11. The food article in this case is 'patisa' which falls in the category of 'sweets'.
This food article is not a standardized food article and does not fall in any of the specified categories as per Appendix-B of PFA Rules.
As such, it is a proprietary food as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules for which no standards have been prescribed under the Act.
Even the PA in his report Ex. PW-1/G analysed the food article as a proprietary food only.
12. The incriminating matter in this case is synthetic food colour Tartrazine.
The PA found the total dye content to be 15.22 ppm.
As per the standards applied by the PA, the total dye content should have been not more than 100 ppm.
13. Rule 28 of PFA Rules enlists the synthetic food colours that are permitted to be used in food articles.
Rule 29 prescribes the food articles where such prescribed food colours can be used.
Rule 30 prescribes the maximum limit in which the prescribed food colours can be used in the prescribed food articles.
14. 'Sweets' has been mentioned in Rule 29(b) of PFA Rules in which such permitted food articles can be used.
Tartrazine is a permitted food colour as mentioned in Rule 28.
As per Rule 30, such food colour is permitted up to 100 ppm.
The food colour in the present case is only 15.22 ppm which is well within limits.
Therefore, as far as the quality, nature or substance of the food article is concerned, there is no violation of any Rule and the product is as per standards.

This is precisely the In Re vs Sh. Sumit Tiwari on 31 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82354384/
3 reason why the PA did not opine the food article to be adulterated.
15. Section 2(ix)(e), under which the accused is facing the trial, states that an article of food shall be deemed to be misbranded if false claims are made for it upon the label or otherwise.
16.

sentences.text: Apparently, the accused is not facing trial for violation of section 2(ix)(d) that applies when the food article is so coloured, flavoured, coated, powdered or polished that the fact that the article is damaged is concealed or when the article is made to appear better or of greater value than it really is.

Similarly, the prosecution has not been launched alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act which applies when the article sold by a vendor is not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser or to his prejudice, or is not of the nature, substance or quality which it purports or is represented to be.
17. It is a matter of record that the food article in this case was lying in an open condition in an open tray.
There was no sealed or closed packet containing the food article.
It was thus not a prepackaged food as defined in Rule 2(t) of PFA Rules.
As such, the food article was not governed by the Packaging and Labelling standards as prescribed in Part-VII of PFA Rules that applies to prepackaged food only.
Therefore, there was no question of any label declaration on such food article being sold in open and loose condition.

18. The only question to be decided is, if any "false claim" had been made for the food article by the accused "otherwise" than on the label, so as to bring the matter within the purview of section 2(ix)(e) of the PFA Act.
19.
The only material available with the prosecution in this regard is Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B wherein the accused / vendor had disclosed the ingredients of the food article.

As per the endorsement made by the accused, the food article Patisa was prepared by using besan, maida, sugar, vanaspati,
soyabean refined, haldi powder, elaichi dana, magaj and pista.
Ld. SPP submits that the vendor did not disclose the use of synthetic food colour tartrazine and such a concealment would amount to a false claim.

20. However, in my considered view, such omission would not amount to a false claim by an accused, particularly when the use of such colour is permitted and the quantity of such food colours was well within the permissible limits.

Rule 24 of PFA Rules requires that where an extraneous colouring matter has been added to any article of food, there shall be displayed one of the prescribed statements in capital letters, just beneath the list of ingredients on the label attached to any package of food so coloured.
It is also provided that where such a statement is displayed, the colour used in the product need not to be mentioned in the list of ingredients.

Thus, when such food colours are used in a food article, a person is not even required to mention the name of the colour and is only required to mention on the label that the food "contains permitted synthetic food colours" in capital letters.
But even this requirement is applicable to only those cases where the food article is being sold in packed condition and having a label.
Where the food article is not in packed condition and there is no requirement of any label on loose and open sweets, this Rule would not apply.

In Re vs Sh. Sumit Tiwari on 31 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82354384/
4 21.

Since there was no label declaration on the food article and no such label was even required to be there on such food article being sold in an open and loose condition, there was no positive and overt act on the part of the accused while disclosing the ingredients.
There is nothing in the testimony of the witnesses to the effect that the FI required the vendor accused to disclose all the ingredients of the food article.

Violation of section 2(ix)(e) might have been there if the vendor had specifically claimed that the food article was not having any food colour in any quantity whatsoever or had claimed that some other food colour was there or had concealed some ingredient which was otherwise prohibited from being used in such food article.
The FI never demanded the food article free from food colours from the vendor nor the vendor claimed anywhere, whether on label or otherwise, that there was no food colour in the food article.
Further, the quantity of food colour detected was very minimal of 15.22 ppm when the permitted range goes up to even 100 ppm.
Such insignificant quantity, even if omitted to be disclosed, cannot be said to be of such value that may be called as a "false declaration" giving rise to a criminal offence.
22. In view of this discussion, the accused deserves to be given benefit of doubt.

The material is not sufficient to conclude that the accused sold a misbranded food article in violation of section 2(ix)(e)
of PFA Act by making some false claim.
23. Having said so, the accused is acquitted of the charges.

His bail bond shall however remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
24.
File be consigned to the record room.

Announced in the open court this 31st day of January 2017 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
